extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in classical literary theory, comedy, and ethics (students, clergy, scholars of Poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository analysis of Aristotle's account of comedy in the Poetics and its ethical role; explicates what counts as comic (character, plot, effect) and practical moral limits on ridicule. Useful for those studying or composing comedy from a classical/theoretical perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as imitation of characters of a lower type
rubrics_metrics.description: “Comedy is... an imitation of characters of a lower type - not, however, in the full sense of the word bad, the ludicrous being merely a subdivision of the ugly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should imitate everyday or lower-type characters rather than noble or royal figures; the comic register targets less exalted characters. This establishes who is a fitting object for comic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic defect (hamartia) rather than destructive flaw
rubrics_metrics.description: “It consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic analogue to tragic hamartia is a defect or error that produces ridicule without causing real harm or destruction. Examples: a distorted/ugly comic mask that implies no pain. When composing or judging comedy, ensure the error remains non-painful and non-destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of plot unity and beginning–middle–end
rubrics_metrics.description: “The various rules about unity and about the sequence of beginning-middle-end apply as much to comedy as to tragedy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should observe coherent plot structure (unity and a clear sequence). Comic works are not structurally lax; they should have an organized plot arc similar to tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy effects a catharsis expressed as laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: “Comedy provides also a certain catharsis of the emotions, expressed not in pity and fear but in laughter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The emotional aim of comedy is a purgation or relief via laughter. Evaluation or creation of comedy should consider whether it produces this cathartic laughter rather than tragic emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy is a subdivision of the ugly (not uplifting/beautiful)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Comedy is a subdivision of the ugly... There is no such thing, for Aristotle, as uplifting or beautiful comedy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic aesthetics embrace the ridiculous or ugly rather than the beautiful or uplifting. Do not expect comedy, in this Aristotelian sense, to aim primarily at beauty or ennoblement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate social status of comic characters (no aristocrats)
rubrics_metrics.description: “First, comedy imitates characters of the lower type, not nobles and kings as in tragedy. No Greek aristocrat is a fit object of comedy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose characters of lower social standing or ordinary condition as subjects of comedy; high-status figures are traditionally inappropriate targets within this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for universalized themes and plots over mere lampoon
rubrics_metrics.description: “Crates was the first who abandoning the ‘iambic’ or lampooning form, universalised his themes and plots.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy has developed when it moves from local lampooning to more universal themes and plots. Good comic writing aims for universality and recognizable situations rather than mere personal invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's ethical function: achieving the mean about the ridiculous
rubrics_metrics.description: Masahiro Kitano's reading of Aristotle/Nicomachean Ethics: comedy helps achieve the ethical 'middle' concerning the ridiculous by purging comic emotion and steering between excess and deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy can serve moral education by moving audiences toward the mean between excessive ridicule and oversensitivity. When evaluating comedy, consider its role in cultivating tasteful moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — buffoon: excess in ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Buffoons, ‘who itch to have their joke at all costs, and are more concerned to raise a laugh than to keep within the bounds of decorum and avoid giving pain to the object of their raillery’ (Nicomachean Ethics 1128a6-7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid comic excess that aims for laughs regardless of decorum or harm; critics should note when comedy crosses into gratuitous cruelty or shameless mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — boorishness: deficiency in comedic engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The boorish and morose, ‘who never by any chance say anything funny themselves and take offence at those who do’ (Nicomachean Ethics 28a7-9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the opposite defect of being humorless or hypersensitive; a healthy comedic culture requires the ability both to make and to receive jokes within decorous bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal comedic virtue: witty/versatile jesting with good taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘middle’ is the witty or versatile, ‘who jest with good taste’ (28a9-10); the person ‘will say and allow others to say to him only the sort of things that are suitable to a virtuous man and a gentleman.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comedic ideal is tasteful wit—joking in ways appropriate to a virtuous person and allowing reciprocal jesting. Evaluate comedy for tasteful versatility and mutual decorum.
